name: Carb cycling

chain: Alternating high and low carb days
Fuel for training, lower weekly calories
angle.text: Physique athletes and lifters use carb cycling to fuel hard training while dieting, aiming for fat loss with muscle kept. Direct trial evidence for advantages over steady dieting is limited, and claims about leptin come largely from practitioners.

summary: Alternating high- and low-carb days around training; popular with physique athletes, with little direct trial evidence.
note: Direct research is limited; not advised without professional guidance for diabetes or eating disorders.
currentQuick:
Carb cycling means alternating days or periods of higher carbohydrate intake with lower-carbohydrate ones, usually putting the higher days on hard training days. It emerged in bodybuilding and spread to the wider fitness audience in the 2010s and 2020s.
Proponents say it supports fat loss, muscle retention and training performance. Reference summaries note that direct research on carb cycling itself is limited and that claimed benefits are mostly inferred from studies of related low- and high-carbohydrate diets.
How it works: Carbohydrate is stored as glycogen, which is held with water. High-carb days refill glycogen and its bound water; low-carb days draw glycogen down and shift fuel use toward fat. Scale-weight swings between days are largely attributed to this water.
Risks and caveats: Described as generally safe short term for healthy people, but long-term effects are understudied. Sources advise professional guidance for people with diabetes, eating disorders or metabolic conditions.
deepLead:
Carb cycling, or carbohydrate cycling, is a dietary approach that alternates days or longer periods of higher carbohydrate intake with lower-carbohydrate periods, commonly scheduling the high-carbohydrate days around intense training . Followers use it for fat loss, retaining muscle and training performance.
The approach is described as originating in bodybuilding in the late 1980s and became widely popular with fitness influencers and online communities in the 2010s and 2020s . Reference summaries state that direct research on carb cycling is limited and that its proposed benefits are inferred from studies of low- and high-carbohydrate diets .

name: Refeed days / diet breaks

angle.text: Dieters schedule refeeds or diet breaks during a cut to look fuller and sustain fat loss. They are common in bodybuilding and appearance-focused circles; research on them is thin and metabolic claims are mostly anecdotal.

summary: Planned higher-calorie days or weeks during a cut; popular in physique circles, thinly sourced here.
note: Few sources were available; effects on appearance are untested here.
currentQuick:
Refeed days and diet breaks are planned periods of increased food intake, often extra carbohydrate, inserted into a calorie-restricted diet. People who diet for a lean look use them in the belief that they aid adherence, training and fullness of the muscles.
Because carbohydrate is stored with water, a refeed can raise scale weight and change how full or flat the physique looks.
How it works: Proponents attribute benefits to restoring glycogen and moderating hunger and hormonal responses to dieting. Glycogen is stored with roughly three to four parts water, which accounts for short-term weight changes.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks are mainly practical, such as stalling the calorie deficit or triggering overeating. People with eating disorders are generally advised against rigid diet cycles.
deepLead:
Refeed days and diet breaks are planned periods of higher energy intake, commonly of extra carbohydrate, within a longer calorie-restricted diet. A refeed usually lasts a day or two, while a diet break lasts longer, such as a week at maintenance intake. They are discussed in bodybuilding and appearance-focused dieting communities.
Proponents say they help dieters stick to a plan, support training and counter hunger. The wiki's reference material for this entry is limited, and no clinical study on appearance outcomes was located. One physiological detail that is documented is that glycogen is stored with water, so carbohydrate intake changes can shift scale weight in the short term .

name: Sodium/potassium manipulation (peak week)

chain: Shifts in water under the skin
Drier, more defined look on the day
angle.text: Bodybuilders adjust sodium, potassium and fluids in the final days before a show or shoot to look drier and more defined. It is documented as part of contest prep; controlled evidence for the visual effect is limited.

summary: Bodybuilder-style salt and water adjustments before a show or shoot; documented as part of contest prep, with associated health risks.
note: Dehydration and electrolyte shifts have documented health risks.
currentQuick:
Peak week is the final stretch of bodybuilding contest preparation, in which competitors adjust carbohydrate, water and electrolyte intake to look more defined on stage. Some appearance-focused people borrow the idea for photo shoots.
Available reference sources describe the general approach only briefly, and no controlled study of the sodium and potassium aspect was found.
How it works: Proponents say altering sodium, potassium and water intake changes how much fluid sits under the skin and in muscle. Carbohydrate loading in the final stage is described as refilling glycogen, which holds water.
Risks and caveats: Intentional dehydration is among practices linked in reference material to higher death rates among bodybuilders. Dehydration of even a few percent of body water can impair cognition and cause dizziness, and larger losses are dangerous.
deepLead:
Sodium and potassium manipulation during peak week refers to deliberate changes to salt, potassium and fluid intake in the days before a bodybuilding contest or photo shoot, with the stated aim of a drier, more defined look. It is part of the final contest-prep stage, which reference sources describe as combining carbohydrate loading with dehydration .
The wiki found no controlled studies of the sodium or potassium protocols themselves. Reference material notes that intentional dehydration is among practices associated with elevated mortality among bodybuilders , and medical sources describe the effects of dehydration .

name: Water cutting / dehydration pre-photo

angle.text: Competitors and photo-minded users restrict fluids shortly before a shoot or contest to look drier and more defined. It appears as the last stage of bodybuilding prep; the visual benefit is reported by practitioners rather than measured in trials.

summary: Restricting fluids to look drier or sharper for a photo; dehydration has well-documented health risks.
note: Dehydration impairs cognition and can be dangerous at larger losses.
currentQuick:
Water cutting means deliberately limiting fluids, sometimes alongside other measures, shortly before a photo, show or weigh-in so the body looks drier and more defined. It originates in physique sport and is sometimes discussed in appearance communities.
No studies of its effect on appearance were found, while the health effects of dehydration are well documented.
How it works: Proponents say less water under the skin and in tissues gives a tighter, more defined look. Body water loss reduces blood volume and tissue hydration.
Risks and caveats: Medical sources report that losing 1 to 2 percent of body water can impair thinking, 5 to 8 percent can cause fatigue and dizziness, and losses above 10 percent can cause serious decline. Reference material links intentional dehydration to higher death rates among bodybuilders.
deepLead:
Water cutting, or pre-photo dehydration, is the practice of intentionally limiting fluid intake in the hours or days before a photograph, contest or weigh-in in order to look drier or more defined. It is described as part of the final stage of bodybuilding contest preparation, which combines carbohydrate loading with dehydration .
Medical references describe dehydration as causing thirst, headache, fatigue and reduced urination, with cognitive impairment from losses of 1 to 2 percent of body water and life-threatening effects at much larger losses . Reference material lists intentional dehydration among practices linked to higher mortality among bodybuilders . No studies of its appearance effects were found.

name: Whole-food / unprocessed diet

angle.text: Users switch to minimally processed foods hoping for leanness, less facial bloating and better skin. Observational studies link ultra-processed food to weight gain and health outcomes; no trials test skin or face appearance.

summary: Cutting ultra-processed food in favour of minimally processed eating; observational links to health outcomes, no appearance trials.
note: The ultra-processed food concept is debated; appearance effects are untested.
currentQuick:
A whole-food or unprocessed diet avoids ultra-processed products in favour of foods close to their natural form. Appearance-focused communities adopt it for skin, leanness and facial puffiness.
Observational studies link high ultra-processed food intake with obesity and several diseases, but the category is debated and no study has tested appearance outcomes of cutting it.
How it works: The NOVA classification groups foods by degree of industrial processing. Proposed links to outcomes include energy density, additives and eating patterns, though reference material says mechanisms are unclear.
Risks and caveats: No notable harms are documented for eating whole foods; critics of the UPF concept note some processed foods are nutritious and that broad condemnation may be oversimplified.
deepLead:
A whole-food or unprocessed diet emphasises foods in minimally processed form and limits ultra-processed foods (UPFs), a category defined by the NOVA classification proposed by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of São Paulo in 2009 and 2010 . In looksmaxxing communities it is promoted for general health, leanness and skin or face appearance.
Observational meta-analyses link higher UPF consumption with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and mortality, but critics say the concept is poorly defined and the evidence largely observational . No study was found on how cutting UPFs affects facial or skin appearance.

name: Clean eating

angle.text: Clean eating, the chicken, rice and broccoli staple, is used in forums for clearer skin and a leaner look. Its health effects have limited research and links to disordered eating have been flagged; skin claims are mostly anecdotal.

summary: A whole-foods eating style (the chicken, rice and broccoli staple) that forums link to clearer skin and leaner looks; research on its health effects is limited and has flagged links to disordered eating.
note: Studies have associated strict clean-eating beliefs with disordered-eating symptoms in some people.
currentQuick:
Clean eating is an umbrella term for diets built around whole, minimally processed foods and avoiding refined sugar, additives and convenience products. It began in 1990s bodybuilding, where it meant high-protein, low-carbohydrate meals such as chicken, rice and vegetables, and later spread through wellness books and social media.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a baseline for leanness, skin and hormones. Researchers have described the scientific literature on clean eating as thin, with most studies looking at how people define it and how it relates to body image and eating behaviour.
How it works: Practitioners favour whole foods, simple ingredient lists and less added sugar, sometimes with extra exclusions such as gluten or dairy. Forum users link this to lower insulin spikes, steadier hormones and fewer acne flares; these mechanisms are discussed in the community and have not been tested as a package.
Risks and caveats: Surveys and qualitative studies have linked rigid clean-eating beliefs with restrained eating and with orthorexia nervosa, a proposed (not formally recognised) eating disorder. Versions that cut out whole food groups have been criticised by commentators for possible nutrient gaps. Analyses of clean-eating blog recipes found nutrient profiles broadly similar to other recipes.
deepLead:
Clean eating is an umbrella term for diets based on the belief that whole, unrefined foods bring health benefits and that processed or convenience foods should be avoided; some versions also exclude gluten, grains or dairy . The term is described as emerging in 1990s bodybuilding, where it meant high-protein, low-carbohydrate eating that avoided sugar and junk food in order to build lean muscle, and as broadening in the 2000s through a series of "Eat-Clean" books by Tosca Reno and later wellness bloggers and influencers .
In looksmaxxing forums the phrase often stands for a plain staple of lean meat, rice and vegetables, and is discussed in connection with body composition, skin and hormone levels . Proponents treat it as a foundation for appearance; the wider wiki entries on diet and skin cover specific foods.
Published research is limited. Wikipedia notes that there is limited research on the health effects of clean eating and that its popularity grew largely through media and anecdote . Studies that do exist mostly examine how people define clean eating, its social media presence, and its associations with disordered eating .

name: Eat the rainbow / skin nutrient diet

angle.text: Users eat varied colourful produce for vitamins and antioxidants, hoping for better skin. Carotenoid intake has been linked to skin colour, while antioxidant supplement trials showed no benefit; the colour approach itself has no skin studies.

summary: Eating many colours of produce for antioxidants in hope of better skin; antioxidant supplements have shown no benefit or small harms in trials, and no skin studies of the colour approach were found.
note: Food-based advice differs from high-dose antioxidant supplements, which have raised safety concerns in some trials.
currentQuick:
Eat the rainbow is the idea of eating fruit and vegetables of varied colours, which contain different pigments and antioxidants, to support health and skin. It is discussed in skin communities as a nutrient-focused approach.
Wikipedia's antioxidant article notes fruits and vegetables are good sources of vitamins C and E and carotenoids, but does not discuss skin, and reports that antioxidant supplements in trials showed no effect or a small mortality increase in vulnerable groups.
How it works: The proposal is that antioxidants and pigments such as carotenoids counter oxidative stress in the skin. Wikipedia notes that laboratory-only antioxidant measures such as ORAC are no longer considered relevant to human diets.
Risks and caveats: Whole produce is generally not the concern; high-dose supplements are. The CARET trial found higher lung cancer rates in smokers taking beta-carotene and vitamin A.
deepLead:
Eating the rainbow refers to eating produce in a variety of colours for the range of nutrients and pigments they contain. Wikipedia describes fruits and vegetables as good sources of vitamins C and E and of carotenoids, noting cooking can destroy some vitamins while raising the availability of some carotenoids .
In skin-focused communities the approach is discussed as a way to improve complexion through antioxidants. Wikipedia's antioxidant article does not address skin, and reports that trials of antioxidant supplements found no effect or a small increase in mortality in elderly or vulnerable groups .
No studies of colour-variety diets for skin appearance were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Oatmeal / fibre for gut-skin axis

angle.text: Users eat oats and other fibre to feed gut bacteria in the hope of clearer skin, via a proposed gut-skin axis. Fibre has documented gut and cholesterol effects; skin benefits are untested.

summary: Eating oats and other fibre to feed gut bacteria in hope of clearer skin; fibre has documented gut and cholesterol effects, but skin benefits are untested in the sources reviewed.
note: Large amounts of some isolated fibres can cause gas and bloating.
currentQuick:
The idea is that fibre-rich foods such as oatmeal feed gut bacteria, which produce short-chain fatty acids and support a healthier gut, with downstream benefits for skin. It is a common gut-skin axis talking point in appearance communities.
Wikipedia describes dietary fibre research as preliminary overall, with associations such as lower cardiovascular risk and relief of constipation, and notes oat beta-glucan lowers LDL cholesterol. The page does not discuss skin outcomes.
How it works: Fermentable fibres are broken down by large-intestine bacteria into short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate, acetate), which are linked to gut-barrier and immune functions.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes inulin can cause flatulence and digestive distress above about 15 g per day, and isolated fermentable fibres may cause bloating and gas.
deepLead:
Dietary fibre is the portion of plant food not fully broken down by human digestive enzymes, including cellulose, resistant starch and pectins . Oats and barley contain beta-glucan, a soluble viscous fermentable fibre that has been shown to lower LDL cholesterol with regular intake .
In the gut-skin axis idea discussed in appearance communities, fibre is thought to help skin by feeding gut bacteria that make short-chain fatty acids . Wikipedia notes that these acids are linked to gut-barrier and immune functions, but describes fibre research as preliminary and does not discuss skin health .
No studies of oatmeal or fibre for skin appearance were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Probiotics / fermented food for skin

angle.text: People take probiotics or eat kefir and kimchi hoping to clear acne and calm skin, based on a proposed gut-skin link. Acne research is described as preliminary, with some evidence in eczema.

summary: Probiotic supplements and fermented foods such as kefir and kimchi, used in hopes of clearer skin; acne research is described as preliminary.
note: Benefits are strain-specific; people with weakened immunity face higher risks.
currentQuick:
Probiotics are live microorganisms that, in the WHO's 2001 wording, confer a health benefit when given in adequate amounts. Fermented foods such as yogurt, kefir, kimchi and sauerkraut contain live cultures, and both foods and supplements are discussed in skin communities for acne and inflammation.
Wikipedia describes the use of probiotics and synbiotics for acne as preliminary research, with possible reductions in inflammatory lesions and improved barrier function. For eczema, the American Academy of Dermatology does not recommend probiotics for established atopic dermatitis.
How it works: The proposed idea is a gut-skin axis in which gut bacteria influence systemic inflammation and the skin. Wikipedia notes that benefits are strain-specific and cannot be assumed across strains, and that gut-microbiome research relies heavily on animal models and small human studies.
Risks and caveats: Probiotics are generally considered safe, but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in critically ill or immunocompromised people. Common side effects at higher amounts include bloating and gas. EFSA has rejected probiotic health claims for insufficient evidence.
deepLead:
Probiotics are live microorganisms defined by the WHO in 2001 as conferring a health benefit on the host when administered in adequate amounts; the European Food Safety Authority rejects that definition because it builds in an unmeasurable health claim . Fermented foods such as yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and kombucha contain live cultures and have been eaten for centuries .
In skin and looksmaxxing circles, probiotic supplements and fermented foods are discussed as a way to improve acne and complexion through the gut. Wikipedia describes probiotics and synbiotics for acne as in preliminary research, noting possible reductions in inflammatory lesions and inflammatory markers .
Published evidence specific to fermented food and skin appearance was not located in the sources reviewed for this entry.

name: Gut health protocols (gut-skin axis)

chain: Eliminating triggers, adding probiotics and fibre
angle.text: Users bundle food elimination, probiotics, fermented foods and fibre to clear skin through the gut. Gut-skin links are mostly associations; no trials of the bundled protocols were found.

summary: Combined elimination and probiotic routines aimed at clearer skin via the gut; the underlying gut-skin links are mostly associations, and no trials of the bundled protocols were found.
note: Strict elimination diets can cause nutrient gaps; probiotics carry rare infection risks in vulnerable people.
currentQuick:
Gut health protocols combine steps such as removing suspected trigger foods, adding probiotics or fermented foods and eating more fibre, with the aim of improving skin through the gut. They are discussed in skin communities under the label gut-skin axis.
Wikipedia describes gut-brain axis research as heavily reliant on animal models and small human studies, with associations considered correlational rather than causal. Its pages on elimination diets and probiotics describe more limited, specific evidence.
How it works: The proposed pathway is that gut bacteria and their metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids affect immune and inflammatory signalling that could reach the skin. Wikipedia notes unresolved causality and large person-to-person variation in microbiota.
Risks and caveats: Elimination diets need to remain nutritionally complete and strict forms are generally not recommended in pregnancy. Probiotics are generally considered safe but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in immunocompromised people.
deepLead:
Gut health protocols for skin typically bundle elimination of suspected trigger foods with probiotics, fermented foods and fibre. The shared premise is a gut-skin axis in which gut microbes influence skin through immune and metabolic signalling.
Wikipedia's account of the related gut-brain axis states that much of the research is in animals, human studies are small, and links to conditions are considered correlational rather than causal; it does not discuss skin . Elimination diets are an established diagnostic tool for food allergy, and probiotics for acne are described as preliminary research .
No studies of combined gut-health protocols for skin appearance were found.

name: Elimination diet

angle.text: Appearance communities use elimination diets to hunt for foods that set off acne or flare-ups, then reintroduce them one at a time to confirm. The method is established for diagnosing food allergy; trials on finding skin triggers are limited.

summary: Temporarily removing suspected trigger foods, then reintroducing them one at a time; established for diagnosing food allergy and eosinophilic esophagitis, with little trial evidence for finding skin triggers.
note: Strict versions can cause nutrient gaps and are generally done with dietitian guidance; people with a history of severe reactions need medical supervision.
currentQuick:
An elimination diet removes suspected foods for a period (roughly two weeks to two months in Wikipedia's description), tracks symptoms, then reintroduces foods one at a time to see whether symptoms return. It is mainly a diagnostic procedure for food allergy and food intolerance.
In looksmaxxing communities it appears as a way to find foods that worsen acne or skin. Medical evidence for elimination diets is strongest in gut conditions such as eosinophilic esophagitis; studies of skin triggers via this method are not in the research reviewed here.
How it works: Foods suspected of causing reactions are cut out, a symptom and food diary is kept, and foods are challenged back in sequence. For allergic or intolerance conditions this tests whether a specific food drives symptoms.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes the diet must be nutritionally complete, symptoms may briefly worsen at the start, and strict versions are generally not recommended in pregnancy. People with asthma, laryngeal oedema or a history of anaphylaxis may need testing where resuscitation is available. Unvalidated tests such as Vega machine testing have not been shown to be effective.
deepLead:
An elimination diet, also called an exclusion or oligoantigenic diet, is a diagnostic procedure for identifying foods that cause adverse effects, whether from food allergy, food intolerance or other causes. A suspected food is removed for about two weeks to two months while symptoms are monitored, and foods are then reintroduced one at a time .
It is used mainly to diagnose food allergy and chemical food intolerance and occasionally as a treatment diet . Its best-documented clinical role is in conditions such as eosinophilic esophagitis, where six-food elimination diets have been studied in children and adults .
In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned as a way of finding foods that trigger acne or other skin changes. The studies reviewed here concern gut and allergic conditions; no clinical studies of elimination diets for appearance or acne outcomes were found.

name: Low-histamine diet

angle.text: Users follow it to reduce facial flushing, redness and eczema-type skin symptoms they attribute to histamine. Followers favour fresh food and limit aged, fermented and cured items. The histamine-intolerance concept and its skin benefits are thinly studied.

summary: An elimination diet cutting aged, fermented and stored foods to curb flushing and skin symptoms blamed on histamine; the concept and the evidence are both thin.
note: Histamine intolerance is not a formally recognised diagnosis; symptoms overlap with allergies and other conditions.
currentQuick:
The low-histamine diet limits foods that are high in histamine or thought to trigger its release, such as aged cheese, fermented foods, cured meats and alcohol. It is used by people who attribute flushing, itching, headaches or digestive symptoms to histamine intolerance.
In looksmaxxing discussion it comes up for facial redness and skin. Studies are small and mostly uncontrolled, and the underlying condition is not formally recognised in mainstream medicine.
How it works: The proposed idea is that the enzyme diamine oxidase (DAO) fails to break down dietary histamine in some people, so histamine accumulates and produces symptoms. This link has not been established, and no validated test exists.
Risks and caveats: The main documented concern is restriction itself: food lists differ between sources and some excluded foods may not be high in histamine. Symptoms can overlap with allergies, mast cell disorders and gut disease, which clinicians evaluate separately.
deepLead:
A low-histamine diet is an eating pattern that restricts foods high in histamine, or thought to promote its release or block its breakdown, with the aim of reducing symptoms attributed to histamine intolerance. Reported symptoms include flushing, itching, headaches and digestive complaints . Typical advice is to eat fresh food, avoid stored leftovers, and limit fermented foods, aged cheese, cured meats and alcohol .
In looksmaxxing circles the diet is discussed mainly in connection with facial flushing, redness and skin quality. Histamine intolerance is not a formally recognised diagnosis in mainstream medicine, and German, Swiss and Austrian allergy societies have advised against the term . Research on the diet is limited: the evidence consists mostly of small observational studies and pilot trials, and reviews have noted that published food lists disagree with one another .

name: Paleo diet

chain: Whole foods, no grains or dairy
angle.text: Followers adopt paleo eating for a leaner physique and for less inflammation, built on meat, vegetables, fruit and nuts. Short trials report some metabolic changes; evidence for body composition and long-term appearance outcomes is limited.

summary: A whole-food, no-grain, no-dairy diet built on a contested picture of ancestral eating; short trials show some metabolic effects, long-term evidence is thin.
note: Excludes dairy and grains; reviewers note possible calcium and vitamin D shortfalls.
currentQuick:
The paleo diet builds meals from meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit and nuts and avoids grains, dairy, legumes and processed foods. It is popular in fitness and appearance communities as a whole-food approach to leanness and skin.
Trials are small and short. Wikipedia describes the research quality as poor to moderate, and some anthropologists dispute the premise that it reflects how ancestral humans ate.
How it works: Proponents say it matches human biology as shaped before agriculture. Researchers note that weight loss on the diet has mainly been explained by lower calorie intake and reduced processed food.
Risks and caveats: Reported concerns include lower calcium and vitamin D intake, side effects such as headaches and diarrhoea in one trial, and the cardiovascular associations of high red meat intake.
deepLead:
The Paleolithic or paleo diet is an eating pattern based on foods its proponents believe pre-agricultural humans ate. It emphasises vegetables, fruit, nuts, roots and meat, and excludes dairy, grains, legumes, refined sugar, processed oils and often salt and alcohol .
Versions of the idea date to the 1890s, and it was popularised by Walter Voegtlin in 1975, by Stanley Boyd Eaton and Melvin Konner from 1985, and by Loren Cordain, who trademarked the name in 2002 . In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a whole-food, low-processed approach to skin, leanness and body composition. Wikipedia describes the research quality as poor to moderate, and critics including anthropologists dispute its assumptions about ancestral diets .

name: Whole30

angle.text: People use Whole30 as a one-month reset, aiming for a leaner body, better energy and clearer skin, then reintroduce foods to spot personal triggers. Gains are mostly reported anecdotally; the program has no controlled trials of its own.

summary: A 30-day strict elimination diet of sugar, grains, dairy, alcohol and legumes; popular as a reset, with no controlled trials of its own.
note: Dietitians have criticised its restrictiveness; no studies of the program's health effects.
currentQuick:
Whole30 asks participants to eat only whole foods for 30 days, cutting added sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and legumes, then to reintroduce them one by one. Its founders frame it as a reset for energy, digestion and cravings.
It is used in appearance circles as a clean-eating protocol. Wikipedia notes no studies had examined its health effects, and some dietitians call it too extreme.
How it works: The premise is that removing common trigger foods and reintroducing them reveals individual sensitivities; any weight change is generally attributed to cutting processed foods.
Risks and caveats: Critics highlight restrictiveness and exclusion of whole grains and legumes. The program's own materials and independent studies on physical risk are limited.
deepLead:
Whole30 is a 30-day elimination diet created in 2009 by Melissa Hartwig (now Melissa Urban) and Dallas Hartwig. Participants remove added sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and (in the original version) legumes and soy for a month, then reintroduce foods one at a time to observe effects .
Its founders present it as a reset for energy, digestion, cravings and sleep rather than a weight-loss plan, and discourage weighing or calorie counting . In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned as a short clean-eating protocol for skin and leanness. Wikipedia states that no studies had specifically examined its health effects as of 2019, and some dietitians have criticised its restrictions .

name: Bryan Johnson Blueprint diet

angle.text: Looksmaxxers follow Bryan Johnson's published meal plan as part of a longevity routine aimed at slowing biological aging and keeping a youthful look. The evidence is his own tracked biomarkers; the diet has not been trialled in others.

summary: The mostly vegan, early-eating plan of longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson; widely shared, tested only on himself.
note: Single-person self-reported results; no controlled trials.
currentQuick:
The Blueprint diet is the meal plan Bryan Johnson uses as part of his Blueprint longevity protocol. It is mostly plant-based and eaten early in the day, and he publishes his meals and biomarker results.
It is discussed in appearance communities for skin and aging claims. The results come from one person, and experts say they do not establish slowed aging.
How it works: Johnson says the aim is to lower the biological age of his organs through diet, exercise, sleep and supplements; the diet itself has not been tested separately.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia and other coverage report expert skepticism and some controversy around Blueprint products. No trial data on the diet exist.
deepLead:
The Blueprint diet is the largely vegan eating plan that American entrepreneur Bryan Johnson follows as part of Blueprint, his longevity protocol announced in October 2021 as Project Blueprint and later a company sold under the slogan "Don't Die" . Johnson says his goal is to lower the biological age of his organs, and he publishes his meals, supplements and biomarker results .
Grokipedia describes a plan of three meals ending by 11 a.m., with items such as a vegetable-and-lentil meal, olive oil and a nut-based pudding . No clinical trial has tested the diet, results are self-reported from one individual, and experts quoted in coverage say biomarker changes do not establish slowed aging .

name: Longevity / Blue Zones diets

angle.text: Users copy the eating patterns of long-lived regions in the hope of staying lean and looking younger for longer. The link to youthful skin is drawn from population observation, and the underlying longevity data are disputed.

summary: Plant-leaning diets modelled on regions reported for long-lived residents; popular, but the underlying longevity data are disputed.
note: Age-record reliability has been questioned; no controlled trials.
currentQuick:
Blue Zones diets copy the largely plant-based eating of places such as Sardinia, Okinawa and Nicoya, where residents are reported to live unusually long.
They appear in longevity and appearance discussions. Reviewers note no controlled studies and have challenged the accuracy of the age data.
How it works: The idea is that plant-heavy food, activity, low stress and social ties together support long life; the diet's separate contribution has not been tested.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms are documented; critics focus on weak evidence and commercial packaging of the concept.
deepLead:
Blue Zones diets are eating patterns modelled on regions reported to have unusually many long-lived people: Sardinia, Okinawa, Nicoya in Costa Rica, Icaria in Greece, and later Martinique . They are generally described as predominantly plant-based, alongside physical activity, low stress and social ties .
The idea originated in a 1999 Sardinia study and a 2004 follow-up by Michel Poulain, Gianni Pes and colleagues; Dan Buettner popularised it from 2005 and Blue Zones LLC was formed in 2008 . In looksmaxxing and longevity circles these diets are cited as a model for healthy aging and skin. Critics have questioned the age data, and reviews report no controlled trials of the diets .

name: Orange juice / vitamin C diet

angle.text: Users drink orange juice or take large amounts of vitamin C to support collagen and brighten skin. The collagen role of vitamin C is established; high-intake effects on appearance specifically are untested.

summary: Heavy orange juice or vitamin C intake for skin, resting on vitamin C's collagen role; untested for appearance and sugar-heavy.
note: High doses cause GI effects; juice is high in sugar.
currentQuick:
This practice involves taking in large amounts of orange juice or vitamin C for skin. The idea rests on vitamin C's role in collagen formation.
No studies have tested it for appearance, and orange juice is high in sugar.
How it works: Vitamin C is a cofactor for collagen-building enzymes; whether extra intake beyond adequacy changes skin is untested in this context.
Risks and caveats: Doses above about 3,000 mg/day have caused diarrhea and other gastrointestinal effects, and the US upper level is 2,000 mg/day.
deepLead:
The orange juice or vitamin C diet refers to consuming large amounts of citrus juice or vitamin C, in the belief that it improves skin. Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen synthesis, and this role is the basis for the appearance claims .
No published trial has tested mega-dose orange juice for skin. Wikipedia describes the health value of orange juice as debatable because of its high sugar content , and reference authorities set an upper intake level for vitamin C because large doses cause gastrointestinal effects .

name: Cinnamon / apple cider vinegar shots

angle.text: Home-made apple cider vinegar shots, sometimes with cinnamon, are taken to reduce bloating, aid fat loss and clear skin. These appearance claims are based largely on anecdote, with no high-quality trials behind them.

summary: Diluted apple cider vinegar (sometimes with cinnamon) taken for fat loss and skin; no high-quality trials back the appearance claims.
note: Undiluted or excessive vinegar is reported to damage tooth enamel and irritate the throat.
currentQuick:
ACV shots are small servings of diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes mixed with cinnamon, drunk in the hope of losing fat, reducing bloating or clearing skin.
Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular use affects body weight or blood sugar and lipids, and that health organizations do not recommend it as a therapy.
How it works: Proponents attribute effects to acetic acid, which they say curbs appetite and moderates blood sugar. Published high-quality evidence for these effects in appearance terms was not found.
Risks and caveats: Diluted moderate use is generally described as low-risk. Reported harms include tooth-enamel erosion, throat and esophageal irritation, digestive upset, and burns when applied to skin or eyes. Possible interactions with insulin and diuretics are noted.
deepLead:
Cinnamon and apple cider vinegar (ACV) shots are a home-made drink in which diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes with cinnamon, is swallowed in the belief that it helps with fat loss, bloating or skin. Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting pressed apple juice first to alcohol and then to acetic acid, and is about 5% acetic acid and 94% water.
Claimed benefits include weight loss, blood-sugar and cholesterol control and skin improvement. The Wikipedia article on apple cider vinegar reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular use helps with body weight or with blood glucose and lipid levels, and says major public health organizations and regulators do not recommend it as a therapy. Documented risks of undiluted or excessive use include tooth-enamel erosion and throat irritation.

name: Fat burner supplements

angle.text: Users take multi-ingredient stimulant blends to speed fat loss and get a leaner, more defined look. Efficacy has not been established at the category level, and blends vary widely between products.

summary: Stimulant-heavy supplement blends sold for fat loss; no category-level efficacy data and a documented record of liver injury and adulteration reports.
note: Regulators and reviews report liver injury, undeclared drugs and psychiatric effects with weight-loss supplements.
currentQuick:
Fat burners are over-the-counter supplement blends, often built around caffeine-type stimulants and plant extracts, sold to raise metabolism or cut body fat.
The sources reviewed contain no efficacy data for the category as a whole, and individual ingredients vary widely in how much research exists.
How it works: Marketing generally describes increased energy expenditure or appetite suppression ('thermogenic'). Mechanisms differ by ingredient and are not established for the blends as sold.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia's supplement overview reports that weight-loss products are a leading cause of supplement liver injury, that multi-ingredient products have been linked to more adverse events, and that many products with undeclared drugs were sold for weight loss. They are sold without pre-market approval in the US.
deepLead:
Fat burner supplements are over-the-counter products, usually multi-ingredient stimulant blends, marketed to increase metabolic rate or reduce body fat. They fall within the broader category of weight-loss dietary supplements, which in the United States are regulated under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA): no pre-market approval is required and the FDA generally acts only after a product is on sale.
The Wikipedia overview of dietary supplements reports no efficacy data specific to fat burners. It does report that weight-loss and bodybuilding products most often cause liver injury among supplements, that green tea catechins are among the most implicated ingredients, and that products with multiple ingredients have caused more adverse events than single-ingredient ones.

name: Green tea / EGCG

angle.text: Green tea and EGCG extracts are used as a mild fat-burner to help get leaner. Support comes mostly from lab and animal studies, with human appearance outcomes less established.

summary: Green tea catechin sold as a mild fat-burner; mostly lab and animal evidence, with liver-safety warnings for concentrated extracts.
note: EFSA says 800 mg or more of EGCG daily could raise liver-damage risk.
currentQuick:
Green tea and its main catechin, EGCG, are taken as a gentle thermogenic for fat loss, either as tea or as concentrated capsule extracts.
Most published work on EGCG is laboratory or animal research, and the sources reviewed contain no completed human trial showing an appearance effect.
How it works: EGCG is absorbed in the intestine and metabolised with help from gut bacteria; oral absorption is poor. Cell and mouse studies report anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects, which have not been established in people for appearance.
Risks and caveats: EFSA stated in 2018 that 800 mg or more of EGCG daily could increase liver-damage risk, and green tea catechins are among the ingredients most implicated in supplement-related liver injury. The FDA has sent warning letters to EGCG makers over disease claims.
deepLead:
Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) is the most abundant catechin in tea, a polyphenol formed from epigallocatechin and gallic acid. Dried green tea leaves contain about 7,380 mg per 100 g, far more than black tea, in which most catechins are converted during processing. Green tea and concentrated green tea extracts are sold as mild 'thermogenic' or fat-loss supplements.
Much of the published research on EGCG is laboratory and animal work, for example in diet-induced obese mice. Reviews describe poor oral absorption. Regulators have raised safety concerns about concentrated extracts: the European Food Safety Authority stated in 2018 that daily intakes of 800 mg or more of EGCG could increase the risk of liver damage, and Wikipedia's supplement overview lists green tea catechins among the ingredients most implicated in supplement-related liver injury.
